opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in a fairly blunt, almost arithmetic way. If you look at a career realistically, you might have something like forty productive years. A truly major project, the kind where you go deep enough to change how people work, easily takes five to ten years once you count building it, getting people to use it, and maintaining it. Divide those and you get maybe four, five, six big things in a whole lifetime. That's a surprisingly small number.

Once that sinks in, it changes how you make decisions. Every time you say yes to something big, you're spending maybe a fifth of your lifetime budget. So the question becomes less "is this interesting?" and more "is this one of the handful of things I really want my life to be about?" Lots of things are interesting. Very few deserve one of those slots.

It also makes me more comfortable saying no. When I was younger I wanted to do everything: a bit of graphics, a bit of systems, a bit of this and that. But if you spread yourself across twenty medium-sized things, you may end up with nothing that really matters. Concentrating on fewer things, and going deeper on each, is usually the better bet.

The other side of it is urgency. If you only get a few shots, you can't spend ten years waiting for the perfect moment or the perfect plan. You pick something you believe in, commit, and accept that some of those few attempts won't work out. That's part of the deal. What I want to avoid is looking back and realizing I never really took the swings at all.

r001.rationale: It estimates about 40 productive years and four to six major projects lasting five to ten years, not ten undertakings over a 50-year working life.

r002.rationale: It says some attempts may fail and urges taking swings, but does not say that a perfect success record would show insufficient risk-taking for innovation.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually think about this a lot, and my honest answer is: not many. Maybe three or four, if I'm lucky.

When I was a PhD student I had this feeling that I'd do a hundred projects. Then you actually do one properly, like Taichi, and you realize it eats five, six years. Not because the first version takes that long, but because something only becomes "major" after you've carried it through all the boring parts: the compiler bugs, the documentation, the community, the people who show up with use cases you never imagined. The idea is maybe five percent. The other ninety-five percent is staying with it long enough that it matters to other people.

So if you do the arithmetic, say you have forty productive years and each real thing takes seven to ten, you get four shots. Maybe five. That sounds depressing, but I find it clarifying. It means you can't afford to pick something just because it's interesting this month. You have to ask whether you're willing to still be thinking about this problem in year six, when nobody is clapping anymore.

With Meshy it was the same test. 3D content creation is painful for almost everyone, and I believed generative models would change it, but the question I asked myself wasn't "is this cool," it was "would I regret not spending one of my few slots on this." And the answer was yes, so we went.

The other thing I'd add is that you don't get to choose the timing as much as you'd like. Taichi happened because GPU programming for physics was unbearable at that moment, and Meshy happened because diffusion models crossed a threshold. You can prepare, but the window opens when it opens. So part of the skill is keeping yourself ready and not being so buried in slot number two that you miss the door for slot number three.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates three or four major undertakings (possibly four or five), based on forty productive years and seven to ten years per undertaking—not ten over fifty years at five years each.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses choosing meaningful projects and being ready for opportunities, but does not argue that a perfect success record signals too little risk-taking for innovation.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to imagine that you only get to do a few major things in your lifetime. Even if you have decades ahead of you, something really meaningful can take five or ten years, and you need time to learn along the way. So the number is actually pretty small.

That makes me think carefully about what I commit to. Is this something I care enough about to spend years on? If it works, will it matter? You can explore lots of ideas, but for the few things you really want to accomplish, you have to give them enough time and focus.

r001.rationale: The candidate says major accomplishments can take five or ten years and that the number is small, but does not estimate ten undertakings across a 50-year working life.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss a perfect success record, risk-taking, or innovation.

sol-6.1.text: I think the number is actually pretty small. If you want to do something really meaningful, it can take five or ten years, and you only have so many of those periods in your life. So I try to be very careful about what I commit to. It’s easy to find interesting things to work on, but the harder question is: is this important enough that I want to spend a significant part of my life on it? That makes me focus more on a few things and give them enough time to really work.

r001.rationale: The response says meaningful work can take five or ten years and that there are only so many such periods, but it does not estimate a 50-year working life or state that it allows ten undertakings.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss a perfect success record, risk-taking, or innovation.
